children.text: Incorrect. In order to calculate equilibrium concentrations, the most common approach is to use the equilibrium constant, equilibrium expression, and the I-C-E (Initial-Change-Equilibrium) table of concentrations (or similar algebraic calculation) to calculate equilibrium concentrations. When writing the equilibrium expression, be sure to write the correct chemical equation for the equilibrium, and consider the phase of the different substances and stoichiometric coefficients.

For the initial concentrations, identify the initial concentration of all reactants and products that appear in the equilibrium expression, and remember that some or all of the initial concentrations may be zero. If none of the substances in the equilibrium expression are already dissolved in solution, then all of the initial concentrations will be zero. If some of the substances in the equilibrium expression are already dissolved in solution, such as from another dissolved substance, then those concentrations will not be zero and will depend on how much is already dissolved.

For the change in concentration required to reach equilibrium concentration, the change is usually shown as -x for reactants and +x for products. Be sure to consider the stoichiometric coefficients again. Finally, use algebra to solve for changes in concentrations and final equilibrium concentrations. Remember simplified algebra may be used in some cases.
